source.text:
Practical vs statistical significance. A result can be statistically significant but too small to matter, or practically large but not yet significant. Decide against the MDE and the business value, not just p<0.05.

Significant does not mean 95% likely real. The 5% in alpha is the false-alarm rate among true nulls, not the chance your specific win is false. If only 10% of your ideas truly work and you test at 80% power, roughly 1 in 5 of your significant wins is a false positive (nishbhana.com, applying Bayes to your own win rate).

Inconclusive tests. A fully-powered test that ends inconclusive is valid evidence that the effect is smaller than your MDE, not a failure. Do not extend it hoping for significance (that is peeking). Ship neither, or ship the cheaper/simpler version, and move on. Kohavi: it is of little value to extend a test that is significantly negative after two weeks; fail fast.

Honest reporting and the experiment log. Keep an institutional experiment log: hypothesis, evidence, primary and guardrail metrics, MDE, planned sample and dates, actual result with CI, SRM check, decision, and what was learned. This builds institutional memory so the same losing idea is not re-run, and surprising winners get replicated. At Booking.com scale (1,000+ concurrent experiments) the bottleneck is not running tests but not fooling yourself with them.

14. benchmarks with their samples

Win rates (share of tests that produce a statistically significant winner), each with its source and sample:

Microsoft: about one-third of experiments improved the key metric; in well-optimised domains like Bing 10-20% (Kohavi). Microsoft 33% success, Bing 15% (Kohavi, Crook, Longbotham 2009 / Kohavi, Deng, Longbotham 2014).

Google Ads, Booking.com, Netflix: about 10% (Manzi 2012; Thomke 2020).

Airbnb Search: about 8% (Kohavi).

Harvard's Stefan Thomke and Sourobh Ghosh, meta-analysis of about 20,000 anonymised Optimizely experiments across 1,000+ customers: "just 10% of experiments had a statistically significant uplift for their primary metric" (via Oliver Palmer).

Optimizely's own analysis of 127,000 experiments across 1,100 companies found only 12% win on the primary metric; clients average about 20% across all experiments but only 10% for revenue-tied tests, with a 35-40% conclusive rate (Optimizely, "Get more wins"). Other platform-published win rates: VWO about 14%, CXL/Convert about 20%.

DRIP ecommerce experiment database: 36.3% win rate, 22.1% loss, 41.6% inconclusive; decisive win rate (wins / (wins+losses)) 62.1%; median winner RPV uplift +2.77%, top quartile +5.21% or higher. Higher than industry because DRIP pre-qualifies hypotheses with research.

ConversionTeam, 2,288 audited tests: 19.1% statistically significant winners per test, 50.5% raw winners, 61.1% decisive. Realistic lift sizes: for mature, well-optimised pages, 1-5% lifts are realistic; for early-stage or unoptimised pages, 10-20%+ is possible. Claims of 50%+ should be treated with suspicion and re-tested (discoveredlabs.com; Twyman's law). The winner's curse: tests run on small samples (200 conversions instead of 2,000) produce both false positives and inflated lift estimates, so early-stopped big winners regress hard.

Part B: stage-gated decision guide by monthly order volume

Assumptions: DTC ecommerce, roughly 2-3% site conversion rate, mostly new/anonymous traffic. Orders/month is the binding constraint because conversions per variant drive power.

Band 1: under 30 orders/month

Valid: qualitative research only (session replay, surveys, user testing, customer interviews, analytics funnel review). Best-practice implementation of known fixes. Repairs.

Not valid: any A/B test, A/B/n, bandits, or before/after with statistical claims. You cannot power even a 30% lift in a reasonable window (about 120+ conversions per variant needed).

Do instead: fix what is broken, apply proven LPG/checkout best practices without testing, build the research habit and an experiment log. Interview customers.

Band 2: 30 to 300 orders/month

Valid: bold, big-swing A/B tests on the highest-traffic page (home, hero product, cart), designed to detect 20%+ relative lifts, run 2-4 weeks, fixed sample computed in advance. Micro-conversion primary metrics (add-to-cart, begin-checkout) with purchase as guardrail. Sequential before/after only for large structural changes with conditions held constant.

Not valid: tweak tests (button colour, minor copy) that need a small MDE; A/B/n; revenue-per-visitor as primary metric (needs about 6x traffic); price A/B tests on the same SKU.

Do instead: one big test at a time, research-heavy. Use a sample-size calculator before every test. Accept that most months you learn from research, not from a powered test.

Band 3: 300 to 3,000 orders/month

Valid: regular A/B tests targeting 10-20% lifts on high-traffic pages; conversion rate as primary metric; guardrails on AOV/margin/return rate; two-week minimum runtime; SRM checks. Sequential/always-valid engines (Statsig, GrowthBook, Eppo, Optimizely) so you can monitor without peeking penalties.

Borderline: revenue-per-visitor as primary (still under-powered unless near the top of the band); A/B/n with only 2-3 arms; CUPED if you have returning identified users.

Not valid: detecting sub-5% lifts; many simultaneous variants; same-SKU price tests.

Do instead: build a prioritised backlog (PXL or profit-weighted), one to a few tests running, disciplined experiment log.

Band 4: 3,000 to 20,000 orders/month

Valid: A/B/n (multi-variant), bandits for short campaigns and tactical high-volume decisions, revenue-per-visitor with winsorization, CUPED, segment analysis (pre-registered), device/source splits. Detecting 5-10% lifts becomes feasible on hero pages.

Not valid: still cannot reliably detect sub-2-3% lifts without long runtimes; still avoid same-SKU price discrimination.

Do instead: run a proper experimentation programme, server-side for checkout/pricing logic (Plus), hybrid A/B + bandit, formal guardrails and stopping rules.

Band 5: 20,000+ orders/month

Valid: full programme. Small-MDE tests (2-5%), revenue and gross-profit-per-visitor primaries, CUPED and variance reduction, always-valid sequential monitoring, multiple concurrent experiments with FDR control, bandits for personalisation, holdouts for surprising winners, long-term novelty/primacy analysis.

Not valid: naive same-SKU price discrimination (ethics/legal), unplanned peeking, uncorrected multiple comparisons.

Do instead: operate like Booking/Microsoft in miniature: institutional experiment log, replication of surprising results, A/A tests to validate the platform, culture that expects most tests to fail.

Part C: curated source list

Must-capture sources (Tier 1-2)

Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang, Ya Xu. Cambridge University Press, 2020. https://experimentguide.com/ Tier 1/2. Topics: 1,3,6,11,13,14. Why: the canonical text; SRM at Microsoft ~6%, OEC, Twyman's law, novelty/primacy as external-validity threats, day-of-week runtime, from teams running 20,000+ experiments/year.

How Not To Run an A/B Test. Evan Miller. evanmiller.org, April 18 2010. https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run-an-ab-test.html Tier 2. Topics: 1,3. Why: the 26.1% peeking false-positive figure, the peek-count-to-required-significance table, and the n=16 sigma^2/delta^2 sample-size rule.

Simple Sequential A/B Testing. Evan Miller. evanmiller.org, October 13 2015. https://www.evanmiller.org/sequential-ab-testing.html Tier 2. Topics: 3,4. Why: a hand-computable sequential stopping procedure for low-conversion settings that ignores failure counts.

Always Valid Inference: Bringing Sequential Analysis to A/B Testing. Johari, Koomen, Pekelis, Walsh. arXiv 2015; Operations Research 70(3) 2022. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.04922 Tier 2. Topics: 3. Why: the mSPRT method behind Optimizely/Netflix/Amplitude always-valid p-values; the peeking-safe alternative to fixed horizons.

Choosing a Sequential Testing Framework. Spotify Engineering (Mårten Schultzberg et al.), March 2023. https://engineering.atspotify.com/2023/03/choosing-sequential-testing-framework-comparisons-and-discussions Tier 1. Topics: 3,5. Why: maps which real tool uses which method (GST/mSPRT/GAVI/CAA) and states GST is more powerful when you can estimate sample size, AVI safer when you cannot.

Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED). Deng, Xu, Kohavi, Walker. Microsoft, WSDM 2013. Tier 2. Topics: 7. Why: the original CUPED paper; variance reduction using pre-period covariates.

Seven Rules of Thumb for Web Site Experimenters. Kohavi, Deng, Longbotham, Xu. KDD 2014. https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/7950675a13e2c57d79629ce5f0ddf81e3bca3502 Tier 2. Topics: 1,3,6. Why: concrete rules on power, runtime, and trust from large-sample practice.

Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: Five Puzzling Outcomes Explained. Kohavi et al. KDD 2012. https://exp-platform.com/Documents/puzzlingOutcomesInControlledExperiments.pdf Tier 2. Topics: 3,6. Why: shows most suspected novelty/primacy trends are statistical artifacts, and when extending a test does and does not help.

Peeking at A/B Tests: Why It Matters, and What To Do About It. Johari, Koomen, Pekelis, Walsh. KDD 2017. https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3097992 Tier 2. Topics: 3. Why: formal treatment of the peeking problem and always-valid fix.

How Etsy Handles Peeking in A/B Testing. Etsy Engineering (Code as Craft), October 3 2018. https://www.etsy.com/codeascraft/how-etsy-handles-peeking-in-a-b-testing Tier 1. Topics: 3. Why: shows false positive rate exceeding 50% after 500 observations under continuous checking at a 50% baseline and alpha 0.10, with a concrete simulation.
